newsitem.title: USA: POLL - US interest rates seen peaking in Q1 '98.
newsitem.headline: POLL - US interest rates seen peaking in Q1 '98.

text.p: Long-term interest rates in the United States are expected to creep modestly higher, peaking sometime in the first quarter of next year, said analysts in a Reuters poll.

Meanwhile, the short end of the yield curve is seen following a similar pattern, with a majority of surveyed respondents projecting an increase in the federal funds target rate before yearend, the survey showed.
Twenty-nine experts forecast on average the two-year note yield would advance steadily to as high as 6.16 percent by February 1998 and ease back slightly to 6.07 percent by August of next year.
Similarly, the experts projected the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond yield would inch up to 6.65 percent by February before slipping back to 6.55 percent a year from now.
That would assume a spread of about 49 basis points between the two issues by February, with that gap holding virtually unchanged through the summer of 1998.
The current spread between the two- and 30-year issues is about 57 basis points.
"I would look for the (yield) curve to get flatter three-to-six months down the road," said Carey Leahey, chief U.S. economist at High Frequency Economics.
Leahey said the short-end of the curve seemed to have gotten ahead of itself recently, when the two-year note closed at 5.74 percent on July 31.
"It meant the market was starting to price in an easing" by the Fed, said Leahey, adding that the economy's current vigor makes such a move highly unlikely.
Heavy selling in the long bond last week caused a slight bulge in the spread between long- and short-term yields, as the back end of the curve underperformed the front end.
But a slimmer yield gap still seems in the cards, said market analysts, citing factors such as the possibility of another interest rate hike and a manageable budget deficit.

"If people think the (Federal Reserve) is going to tighten, that will be more negative for the shorter end, and the longer end will still be helped by the view that inflation numbers will continue to be very good," said Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank.
In a separate survey, 24 of 33 economists polled by Reuters predicted the central bank would rein in credit at least one more time this year, probably in the fall.
However, if inflation continues to remain dormant and the Fed refrains from boosting rates, the entire yield curve could shift downward, analysts said.
Cheryl Katz, a senior economist at Merrill Lynch, said she expected inflation to remain very restrained amid healthy economic growth, resulting in lower rates across the board.
Comparing the current inflation picture with price increases in the late 1950s and 1960s, Katz claimed similarities exist.
But the bond market now offers much higher nominal rates of return because of the market's stubborn perception that inflation may start to rise, she said.

"There is a lot bigger inflation premium when one looks at nominal yields," Katz said. "That inflation premium will start to go down ... which will let nominal rates decline," allowing the long bond yield to hit 6.0 percent a year from now, she said.
Full results of the survey follow.
